newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico peso battered by Greenspan, certification.
newsitem.headline: Mexico peso battered by Greenspan, certification.

text.p: The Mexican peso plunged in late trade to end sharply weaker on Thursday after a speculative onslaught in a skittish market, traders said.

Traders said gains in U.S. long bond yields following Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony on Wednesday coupled with the certification process of Mexico's cooperation in the war on drugs were the main causes of market anxiety.
"Looking at it in the cold light of day, what happened was that speculation snowballed once foreign banks began to dump pesos on stop losses," a dealer said.
The benchmark 48-hour peso and the 24-hour contract closed 17.6 and 17 centavos weaker, respectively at 7.9600/7.9800 and 7.9500/7.9700 per dollar.
Same-day peso contracts had earlier closed 4.9 centavos weaker at 7.8220/7.8250 per dollar.
Banco de Mexico did not intervene in the markets despite the fact an announcement on February 19 that it would inject up to $200 million if the peso slid by more than two percent.
A spokeswoman for the central bank said it only sold dollar put options to local banks until 1215 local time/1315 EST/1815 GMT, or 75 minutes before the foreign exchange market closes.
"Since the peso was not more than two percent weaker at that time, Banco de Mexico did not intervene," said the spokeswoman, who wished to remain anonymous.

In a February 19 release, Banco de Mexico said that if the peso fell more than two percent, it would auction $200 million among banks at a minimum price two percent above the exchange rate of the previous working day.
The spokeswoman was unable to say whether the central bank would sell dollars at the start of trade on Friday.
An analyst said the confusion among traders probably arose as they were considering trading levels as a reference rate, rather then the central bank's official fixing rate.
The fixing rate to be published in Friday's edition of the Mexican Government Official gazette will be 7.8358 pesos per dollar.
This means, the analyst said, that the peso would have to reach a trading rate of 7.9925 per dollar before 1215 local time for the central bank to begin to accept bids from banks to purchase dollars.
Traders said nervousness escalated in late trade.
"Panic gripped the market, dealers began to speak of pesos changing hands at eight per dollar," one trader said.
"Speculators had a field day with Greenspan's testimony, higher U.S. long bond yields and the certification process," he added.
Yields on U.S. 30-year Tresury bonds gained to 6.81 percent in late trade, compared to 6.67 percent before Greenspan spoke on Wednesday.
Among other things, Greenspan said he could not rule out increased U.S. interest rates in order to curb inflationary pressures.
